column2: A dance in which he stands and then falls the next instant; the falls become so violent (bruised hips) that he realizes he is trying to kill himself and must stop. Bruises on the hipbones
A pine plantation brought the college a little money, but the operation as a whole lost money.

For Wes Huss's 45th birthday, the following summer, the potters David Weinrib and M.C. Richards organize a black arts ball; Rumaker and Pat Nelson go dressed as a monk and a nun. Wes Huss's 45th birthday

On a deliciously fragrant evening, Rumaker asks Ellen whether they might make love; she answers only that she will be in her room later. That night he knocks at her window; the room is empty; he feels deceived, his pride wounded, and goes back to his study in the Studies Building. Consequences: He understands that his desire for her was only half sincere and that what he loved above all were her qualities

Rumaker has his literally transcribed adaptation of Dostoevsky's “Grand Inquisitor” read aloud. Duck Daley and Wes criticize it harshly: a mere transcription is not drama; everything dramatic remains in Dostoevsky's prose. Rumaker learns about his vanity and arrogance. The whole text read aloud one evening in class; looks of pitying tolerance from the other students. Consequences: Rumaker feels burned but instructed: he had a great deal to learn.

Back again, Olson learns that Rumaker has worked on “The Grand Inquisitor” and asks to see it. Seeing that nothing has been transformed, he hands the manuscript back at once: discussing it in his class would be throwing him to the wolves. The manuscript handed back right after a quick glance. Consequences: Another lesson learned by Rumaker.

Late winter: women in bonnets and long flour-sack dresses, squatting with burlap sacks, gather wild greens along the road, eaten raw or made into tinctures and tonics. Poke bonnets, flour-sack dresses, gunny sacks, raw greens, tinctures, tonics.

Rumaker opens the door to the terrace and sees a black king snake at least 9 feet long looping over and over on the left-hand railing, shedding its skin; the gray dead skin falls several stories below. Mary Fiore tells him this ritual takes place every early spring. A black snake at least 9 feet long; the scales of the new skin gleaming in the sun; shreds of gray tissue fluttering to the ground. Consequences: Rumaker will see several other king snakes perform the same ritual.

A king snake stretched across the road is run over by the wheels of a big sedan that slows down without seeing it; the snake, even bigger than the others, slides slowly into the marshy grass toward the lake, visibly unharmed. A slow sedan, four wheels, marshy grass by the road, an undulating body.

Olson's return after the winter (he was coming back from an archaeological trip to Yucatán with his wife Connie) lifts everyone's spirits, as if the winter grayness were lifting in them too, on the slopes of the Seven Sisters. A dig among the ancient Maya of Yucatán with Connie, on a shoestring archaeological grant. Consequences: The writing class resumes.

The classes are held in the afternoon in the warmest room of the office cottage; old regulars (“Olson vets”) and newcomers rub shoulders; Olson talks almost all the time, and the veterans toss out questions and comments that Rumaker does not understand; he keeps quiet and absorbs. Paintings by Jack Tworkov, Franz Kline, and Willem de Kooning above the cut-stone fireplace and on the gray walls; Home Run and Picayune cigarettes at 18 cents a pack (no tobacco tax in North Carolina), sold at Carroll Williams's store; Olson chain-smoking his Camels; opening the window even a crack forbidden, since Olson cannot stand a draft. Consequences: Rumaker spends hours in the library with Nell Rice's help learning the vocabulary: Pound, William Carlos Williams, Frobenius (African Genesis), Jung.

A strict requirement: bring a manuscript, or no admission to class. Rumaker has piles of them, those from his trunk and those written on canary yellow second sheets, the cheapest paper at Carroll's store. Canary yellow second sheets, written in his study after his kitchen shifts.

Olson hands back the stories covered with almost indecipherable pencil scribbles; Mary Fiore, the campus expert on Olson's handwriting, helps Rumaker decipher them. The comments, slangy, are contemptuous, sneering even at Rumaker's spelling of “cigaret” for “cigarette”; no praise. Rumaker is crushed and thinks he will never become a writer, but redoubles his work. Pencil scribblings in the margins; mockery of “cigaret”. Consequences: Rumaker listens harder, reads more, works more, joins the “hangers-on” who write to please the master; he will later understand that he was being tested; sometimes one has to be cruel to be kind.

As rumors spread about Rumaker's bad writing, Jorge surreptitiously leaves paperbacks by Edna Best, Kathleen Norris, once Fanny Hurst (lady novelists, in the sense of a macho slur) on his desk, a mocking assessment of his work. Sentimental paperbacks; “Enjoying your Fanny Hurst?” tossed at him with a snicker. Consequences: Continued humiliation.

Jorge reads a poem (influenced by William Carlos Williams and Creeley); Olson asks which are the best lines; after a long silence, Rumaker, who never opens his mouth, quotes: “What do you want / that you would break / your head your heart / to learn”. Olson gives him a surprised look and an approving grin. Rumaker admits he is reconstructing the lines from memory, ~50 years later, with apologies to Jorge. Consequences: Worth all the courage it took Rumaker to speak.

Dick Bishop, a slightly built, bespectacled former serviceman living with his wife and child at the other end of Last Chance, leaves Olson's class to write romances that pay, having bought the only electric typewriter on campus. Olson sneers: it will make him type faster, not write better. A new electric typewriter, the only one on campus; a family settled at the top of the hill. Consequences: Bishop shuts himself in to type, then leaves with his family.

Olson reads from the newly published Pisan Cantos, composed by Pound while confined at St. Elizabeths (begun in 1948 [sic] in the prison camp near Pisa). He is amused by “the moon is my pinup”, Ez' using GI slang to sound hip; he does not buy it. He points to the black Chinese ideogram LING and asks who can “read” it; Rumaker suggests “harmony,” then “Sensibility”; Olson: “Bingo!” A big bold black ideogram in the middle of the text. Consequences: A second moment of grace for Rumaker.

One Saturday afternoon, cutting kudzu and bamboo with bolo knives; during a break, Olson asks Rumaker what he is reading; when he answers Carson McCullers (The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter), he gets a sneer: “Saturday night,” and Olson goes back to the tall weeds. Bolo knives, invasive kudzu, hard, sweaty work. Consequences: Rumaker blushes but goes on reading McCullers in secret, feeling a kinship with her dark, twisted root of queerness, as with Tennessee Williams and Truman Capote, read on the sly because not approved.

Speaking of Malraux's Man's Hope (the Republican battles of 1936-1939), Olson tells with emotion how many young Americans of his generation struggled with the dilemma of dropping everything to join the Lincoln Brigade against Franco, a world seen as balanced between democracy and fascism. He suggests he was long troubled that he had not gone.

Olson persuades Rumaker to write to Yezierska in New York; she answers with several letters in a large, bold hand, saying she had nearly killed herself writing those books, huge in the 1920s with a Hollywood contract from Samuel Goldwyn, but now out of print and forgotten. Letters in a large, bold hand. Consequences: A lesson in style: direct, simple prose with complex content.

Victor Sprague, embittered by Black Mountain and perhaps by too much sour mash, leaves with his wife; the Husses and baby David move into their white board house with dark green trim beyond Mrs. Jalowetz's; the Fiores move into the Minimum House, designed and built by students at a minimal cost of $1,000. Minimum House: one room, a wall of glass looking out on the stream that tumbles through the campus, at the bend of the farm road.

Connie tells Rumaker several times how much she likes the music he plays while doing the dishes; one day when she thanks him in front of him, Olson mocks Rumaker's taste in music, implying he has everything to learn, a need to be the authority on everything, tinged with jealousy; Rumaker would have preferred her to keep quiet in his presence. Consequences: Rumaker gradually discovers Olson's need to dominate.
Coming back from a William Holden movie at the Roxy in Swannanoa, Connie remarks that she finds him “sexy”; Charles, jealous of a celluloid phantasm, immediately disparages Holden as an actor.

One summer dusk after supper, Olson laughs uproariously from the screened porch on the south side of the lake, comfortably slumped in a cane chair, long legs spread, hands on his knees, shouting instructions to Connie, who is trying to pole the old, split community rowboat with no oars, Kate (~2) sitting solemnly in the middle; exasperated, her throat reddening, Connie hitches up her skirts and jumps into the muddy water up to her knees to pull the boat to shore, the thick reeds making the landing narrow and risky. A worn, split community rowboat with no oars; thick reeds; a narrow landing.

In the winter of 1953, a Jungian come from Zurich for Olson's three-week seminar, the “Institute of the New Sciences of Man”; Rumaker shares his dreams with her for interpretation. Three-week seminar, winter 1953. Consequences: Rumaker's Jungian reading, nourished by von Franz and Olson's classes on Jung.

Urged by Olson to write down his dreams (as Jung prescribes), Rumaker dreams: an old Black woman escorts him down a long, squalid corridor and up a staircase; at the top, before a dark door, stands a tall, massive man in a long, voluminous black robe, wearing a black turban adorned with a golden crescent moon, solemn, dignified, silent. The old woman bows, steps back, and beckons him to approach. Interpreted with von Franz: this Wise Old Man, a Jungian archetype, is Olson, spiritual father of Fee and of the lost sons of Black Mountain, likened to the stray dogs that come up from the hills, beaten dogs, fierce from wanting a home (like the pack taken in by “Madame” at Streamside). A voluminous black robe, a black turban with a golden crescent moon, a squalid corridor. Consequences: Rumaker decides he will not lose this second father, having already been thrown out by the first.

The first party at which Rumaker sees Olson: Jorge Fick has brought back the Miles Davis record from Detroit. Olson, hunched over the phonograph, listens intently, demands to know who is playing, and has the record played again. Then he dances number after number with Arlene Franklin. Olson in a high, supple crouch, small steps near the phonograph, his head above his partner's, “like a whale,” Rumaker will say. Consequences: The first and only time Rumaker sees Olson dance.

At noon the day after the party, on an impulse of impertinent affection, Rumaker tells Olson he danced “like a whale,” without thinking of Moby-Dick. Olson, offended, hits him with a sharp punch to the biceps that nearly knocks him off the steps, then says “Oh you!” and goes off to check his mail. Eyebrows shooting up above his glasses; a punch that nearly knocks Rumaker off the steps; burning flesh. Consequences: A lesson for Rumaker: watch his tongue, exactly what Olson demanded in the writing workshop.

In early spring 1953, the two painters and the New York dealer spend a night at the college for a show and lectures, and no doubt so that Kline, the outside examiner for Fick's degree, can look at Jorge's paintings. Kline, relaxed, tells delicious stories around the kitchen stove; Guston is sparing with words. People (Fee above all) hope Kline will come back to teach; he never will. A cold, gray afternoon, coffee drunk at the kitchen stove; a metal-topped table; years later Dan Rice will be able to repeat Kline's shaggy-dog stories word for word. Consequences: Kline's last visit to BMC.

In the spring of 1953, the class climbs the hill to meet on the open deck of the science building that Natasha Goldowski still refuses to occupy; Olson also wanted to show her how ridiculous her fear was that the modernist building on stilts would slide down the slope. A welcome change from the smoky back room of the office cottage. Sprawled on the boards of the deck, pine branches all around, the smell of resin against the smoke of Home Runs and Olson's Camels.

On a gray, rainy afternoon, class indoors. Short of manuscripts, Olson has Rumaker read for the first time: a dreadful story built on his mother's South Philly anecdotes (notably the Irish innkeeper who smeared egg yolk on the mouths of drunks to make them think they had already had breakfast). Olson, furious, tears the text apart: secondhand anecdotes, rehashed leftovers. A whole wall of windows; Rumaker reads in a timid voice. Consequences: A founding lesson: write what you have seen and heard yourself, in your own voice; Rumaker feels exposed, skinless.

Shortly after von Franz's visit, Rumaker writes for the Melville course a critique of “Bartleby the Scrivener,” the first text that really excites and pleases Olson. The course covered Clarel, Melville's stories and novels, Hawthorne, Shelley, Stendhal, D. H. Lawrence, and Williams. Carroll Williams had typed out the whole of Studies in Classic American Literature with carbons, since no edition was available. Olson teases Rumaker about a paper on The Marble Faun: “too Laurentian,” calling Lawrence an American, not an Englishman. The single tattered copy of Studies in Classic American Literature, another BMC “bible,” circulated like a sacred relic; Olson called Pierre “the blonde-brunette novel” and Moby-Dick “a great stew of everything stirred in together” Consequences: The beginning of Olson's literary recognition of Rumaker

After reading Rumaker's text linking Bartleby to the Book of Job, Olson meets him on the road by the lake and declares his excitement: Bartleby is Melville; the story is about Melville's soul, about the artist-scribe in America. He proposes printing a broadside or a pamphlet together at the print shop, including Rumaker's essay and having others contribute. A meeting one afternoon; a printing project at the print shop; the exclamation: “Mike, you must stop hiding your talents under a bushel basket!” Consequences: Olson praises the essay very highly in class; Rumaker earns the cautious respect of the Olson veterans; a lasting change in his relationship with Olson

Olson praises the Bartleby text “skyhigh” in front of the other students, which earns Rumaker acceptance and at least the cautious respect of the seasoned students. Rumaker walked on air for days Consequences: For Olson, Rumaker becomes a student, an accepted apprentice

As a mark of acceptance, Olson lets Rumaker read books in his private study, which he never lent. Strict rules: read only in the study, let no one in, lock the door again on leaving. There Rumaker reads Lady Chatterley's Lover (one of the 1,000 unexpurgated copies printed by Lawrence himself in Florence in 1928) and discovers the works of Jung. A locked study, the only one; wall shelves full, many rare first editions; many books “borrowed” from the college library and never returned, a losing battle for Nell Rice; a paperback collection of Jung given by Mary Fiore also ended up in Olson's collection Consequences: Rumaker sees it as an honor and a sign of trust, including in his writing

Melville's granddaughter Eleanor Metcalf, with whom Olson had become friends through his Melville research, and her husband Harry are invited to the college. One afternoon before dinner, sitting on a cane chair in her purple outfit, she tells her memories of her grandfather. Outfit: a voluminous pleated purple plaid suit with a short cape, a matching Scottish military cap, frizzy silver hair; Olson very courteous, treating her like a favorite aunt Consequences: Rumaker is struck that she saw Melville as a child, in the flesh

She tells of the Melvilles' house in lower Manhattan; her grandparents had separate bedrooms, a snow-white blanket on her grandmother's bed and a deep black one (at his request) on her grandfather's; Melville took the children to the park but was so absorbed that he hardly spoke to them; one day he forgot them on a bench and went home alone, Mrs. Melville crying “Herman! Where are the children?”; a painting of the Bay of Naples in the hall, which Melville pointed to with his cane, singing “See how the little boats swing to and fro, to and fro...” Separate bedrooms with white and black blankets; a cane waved in a rhythmic gesture; a mischievous smile as she mentions the separate bedrooms Consequences: Plenty of material for symbolic readings of Moby-Dick

After Olson's introduction (in which he calls Rumaker's essay on Bartleby “a wonderful piece,” making Rumaker blush), Olson suggests sending the essay to Cambridge; about a week after it is sent, Rumaker receives a gracious letter of thanks. A letter on gray “pussy-willow” paper, as gracious as her smile

Marilyn Monroe in Niagara (her first big role) in Technicolor on an Asheville screen; Olson, visibly smitten, talks about it with verve one evening in class to the boys who have seen the film. Later he will comment that she had only has-beens (DiMaggio, the dullest of baseball players; Arthur Miller), no one up to her measure. A “lascivious flicker” in his eyes; more animated than usual

Olson asserts: “I'm sure that's why the cloacal and the genital are so close a triad in us”, suggesting the closeness of the generative and the eliminative, creation and destruction. Flola Shepard, in the front row, grates skeptically as she often does, but Olson holds his ground. Flola Shepard described as “coldly, passionately logical” Consequences: The sentence sticks with Rumaker for years and resurfaces in a visionary scene of his 1977 novel A Day and a Night at the Baths

One late morning in the summer of 1953, Rumaker climbs to the back doorstep, heart pounding, to talk to Olson about his graduation project. Through the kitchen screen door he sees, down the hall, Charles lying on his bed, barely awake, a sheet folded over his thighs, staring into space, his hand wandering over his plump belly and a thick tuft of black pubic hair. His fists, ready to knock, freeze in midair. Separate bedrooms with Connie (Olson nocturnal, Connie on Kate's schedule); a compact modern house built by the students, formerly the Jalowetzes', just beyond Meadows Inn; Connie and Kate no doubt gone to the stream near the print shop Consequences: Rumaker compares this to the only time he saw his own father naked, as a child

Flashback: at about 11-12, Rumaker sells the Philadelphia Inquirer at dawn to the graying workmen boarding for the Navy Yard; paid half a dollar a morning, often less because customers stole papers; Pete Kelly, an old, arthritic, smelly Irishman, recounted every paper with his knotted fingers and deducted 5 cents for each stolen copy. Then Rumaker walked a mile to serve Mass at St. Matthew's. One winter morning, his father, in the grip of a hangover, had overslept; he burst out in his underwear, leaned over his son, opened the cracked window, the icy air on the boy's back, and shouted to the honking men below that he was coming; Joe Harper threw out a shrill gibe. Rumaker then saw, for the only time, the tuft of black pubic hair on his father, identical to Olson's. Leaving at 5 a.m. on the running board of Pete Kelly's old khaki Chevy (painted during the war); corduroy knickers and long stockings for the boys; six brothers in two beds in a tiny dark room; his father's pride in going to the shipyard despite the Schmidt's beer of the night before, his face gray as death; a lunch kettle; the Camden yard farther up the muddy Delaware Consequences: The physical parallel between father and Olson feeds Rumaker's filial attachment

A tattered copy of a book (by Lawrence, out of print, before the Doubleday-Anchor paperback edition) passed from hand to hand like a sacred relic; Carroll Williams retyped the whole book, with carbons, so that others could read it. Typed out in full with carbons

About a paper by Rumaker on The Marble Faun, Charles reproaches him for sounding “too Laurentian,” amused in front of the others, noting that Lawrence's singular voice is hard to resist, and calling D. H. Lawrence an American, not an Englishman. A critique made in class, with amusement in front of the others

Jalowetz bound the library's books for Nell and taught bookbinding to the Franklin sisters, Phyllis and Arlene, from Kansas; she helped Williams bind the illustrated holograph manuscript of Patchen's Journal of Albion Moonlight; Rumaker, invited by Jonathan (who had lent him the manuscript to read the day before), finds her so nervous and fearful (touch nothing) that he leaves before the end, missing the process he was burning to see Workshop in The Stables, the Franklin sisters from Kansas, an illustrated holograph manuscript

Natasha leaves the college in the fall of 1953, taking Eric and Madame to a small rented farm off the main highway toward Asheville, this side of Beaucatcher Mountain. A rented farm about 15 miles from the college, on the other side of the mountains to the east Consequences: Olson has a free hand to run the college as he likes; the departure is seen as Natasha's defeat in her fight against Olson.

Shortly after they move in, Eric comes to pick up Rumaker and Merrill at the college for their first visit since the three left. A tour of the house, a walk around the land, an introduction to Rougea the cow, a milking in which the two students take part for the first time, a meal, college gossip requested by Madame in French. Unpasteurized, unhomogenized milk, cheese and cottage cheese, whey given to the chickens, cold grass at dusk, a sky full of sun over the western hills, air turned crisp with autumn cold Consequences: Rumaker sees that Natasha has found happiness again and regrets that the college lacks her energy.

A last afternoon and day at Natasha's, freed from the college and from Olson's domineering shadow; Rumaker finds her exuberance wonderful and sad, since the college would have needed it as a counterweight, impossible given Olson's will to be the boss. Eric drives Rumaker and Merrill back to the college. Rented land, but hers; an outpouring of liveliness from Natasha Consequences: Rumaker will never see Natasha, Madame, or Eric again.

For lack of room, Rumaker sets up extra tables from the porch to the veranda of the Round House. At lunch, Kate, on the lap of Olson, who is sitting too far from the table, spills soup and food on the floor. Rumaker gently suggests that Olson move closer; Olson snaps at him, asking what is wrong with him, calling him grandpa. The table falls silent; Rumaker, red-faced, stammers; Olson, sarcastic, says he only wanted to..., staring at him, his face hard with fury; Jorge Fick, his neighbor, sings out mockingly that the baby is going to cry. The Round House's Steinway grand; a floor to be washed; flashback: his father reading the Philadelphia Bulletin, slaps at childhood dinners Consequences: Rumaker sees his father again; shame and shock at the table.

Merrill has not taken any classes since Lou Harrison left, replaced by Wolpe, whom he despises; his cold arrogance offends some; he refuses chores and work, except that once or twice, as a favor to Rumaker, he helped Dan Rice and Cynthia Homire wash the kitchen floor on a Saturday afternoon. Kitchen floor chore, Saturday afternoon Consequences: A growing risk of expulsion.

Jack Rice, the newly hired work coordinator, with his pregnant wife Barbara and daughter Megan, knocks at dawn to roust Merrill for his chore. Merrill ignores him; Rumaker, afraid of being caught in bed with a man, keeps quiet. Jack pushes the door open and finds them entwined on the mattress dragged near the stove the night before for the cold snap. He barks, asking whether Gillespie is on duty that morning. Merrill mumbles and burrows back under the quilt; Jack insists, asking whether he is coming, stares at the bulge, looks at Rumaker, then walks out, slamming the door. The feather-bed mattress near the stove; a cold snap; a black leather jacket, a big buckle, filthy Levi's, work boots, a strawberry-blond crew cut, piercing blue eyes, a former Marine Consequences: Rumaker senses that such incidents will earn Merrill a new request to leave.

After a quarrel with Huss and Olson over the perceived lack of support, Jack, in a fit of testosterone, pins up a six-page ultimatum aimed at Huss and company (exempting Olson). Olson, amused, asks the opinion of those reading over his shoulder; we answer only with smiles and shrugs; Olson says nothing about it publicly. Six pages; the cork board in the entrance of the Studies Building

Merrill wants to do something nice for poor Bea (perhaps to get back at Wes): he himself buys Asian vegetables and condiments in Asheville (a shrimp dish), with Bea in the old dark green Mercury, cooks it himself in the Husses' kitchen, sets the table by the parlor windows, baby David already in bed. As they sit down, Wes comes in without a word, settles into an armchair a few feet away, crosses his long legs, and calmly reads a book on Brecht. Merrill and Bea chat about the dishes, pretending to ignore him; Rumaker, mortified, can hardly swallow and dares not say anything to Wes. Dark green Mercury; a table carefully set by Merrill; an armchair; a book on Brecht; the baby in bed Consequences: A silent victory for Wes through passive resistance (his Quaker heritage and conscientious objection in 1939-45); Rumaker envies his quiet strength and regrets that Merrill does not care as much about his feelings. Merrill will never comment on Wes's presence, able to erase it.

Jerry, a former Marine with a radiant smile, tells, puzzled and flattered, how he met Bea alone in the middle of the night, wandering; after greetings, she supposedly came up to him and touched him, though she had never been more than vaguely friendly. Rumaker notes that if she had seen him sunbathing naked on the deck behind the Studies Building, a habit of Jerry's, that would explain it. “Jesus, it was Wes' wife!”; the Olsons still at the party that night; once Rumaker had followed Jerry, drunk after a party, to his studio in the Stables, without success

After supper, Rumaker, Bert, and Virginia drink jars of Bert's home brew in his cluttered office; Bert and Rumaker, drunk, caress each other in front of Virginia (in love with Rumaker); when she leaves, Bert slams the door and they fall on each other. Bert then avoids Rumaker, to his great confusion. Bags of yeast, crates of full and empty Mason jars, a bookcase, a wall desk, chairs, a pallet; Bert's thighs in threadbare Levi's; knees pressed together Consequences: Rumaker dreams of Bert for weeks, seeing him as a cure for his dry spell since Merrill left; disappointment

To thank Claire and Doyle for welcoming the class into their parlor to watch the McCarthy hearings on television (the “Reading the Newspaper” course), Olson brings the whole class to wash the farmhouse windows; Rumaker at the top of a swaying ladder, Olson below, laughing. A row of back windows, a precarious ladder

With all the free rooms reserved for Summer Institute guests, Rumaker goes back to his bed in the attic dormitory of South Lodge. Consequences: He keeps busy with Wes's theater classes and Cunningham's movement classes

Huss persuades Cunningham, whose company is part of the Institute, to teach a movement class to help the actors' acting, at 8 a.m. after breakfast several mornings a week; Rumaker also tries a few sessions of the advanced class for Merce's dancers, to his amusement. Merce's cry: “Fly across the floor! Fly! Fly!”; Rumaker feels like a chick learning to fly Consequences: A liberating discovery of the body beyond dishwashing, sweeping, and sex

After one of Merce's classes, Mary Ann (who has come to study photography with Hazel Larsen) takes a photograph of Rumaker perched on the railing of the dining hall porch, playful, a nasturtium pinched between thumb and forefinger, a pose parodying the athletic movements he has learned. A nasturtium taken from a vase on the tables

In the afternoon, the company rehearses and takes classes in choreography and theory in the big dining hall with its high, exposed-beam ceiling; Merce choreographs “Septet” to Satie's “Trois Morceaux en forme de poire,” which David Tudor plays on the Steinway over and over, a cigarette in his mouth. Ceramic cups from the Weinribs' pottery, small bouquets of wildflowers on each table, a dish cart, the dancers' muffled bare feet, Merce's short laugh at mistakes Consequences: Rumaker hears Satie for the first time through the open windows

After a rehearsal, Merce talks at length about Ulysses to his dancers sprawled on the floor; Rumaker listens eagerly through the open windows, all the more since Ulysses is anathema in Olson's writing classes (a closed form, a dead end). Rumaker had borrowed Ulysses from the forbidden shelves of the Prendergast Library in Jamestown the summer before BMC Consequences: A convergence as Rumaker sees it: Merce's birdlike body, dance as flight

The company and Cage have thrown a surprise birthday party at Streamside; in the morning Merce arrives late for the 8 a.m. class, gray and disheveled, accompanied by Paul Taylor; the cook Malrey has made no exception for breakfast; Merce apologizes with a sheepish smile and launches into the jumping exercises. Rumor: an unusual amount of wine consumed

Their arrival together at breakfast feeds the gossip of a microcosm obsessed with it; no public indication of who was with whom; Rumaker notes that the members of the avant-garde were already beyond categories of sexuality. Olson's formula recalled: “There are no camps”

Rumaker remembers Merce complaining that more things went wrong there than anywhere else; nevertheless, free space to develop his experimental dances and a temporary freedom from worries about food and lodging. He had already come in 1948.

Cage comes into the dining hall in khaki overalls, with the pale, expressionless face of a moon-faced mountaineer; Rumaker takes him for an assistant to the handyman T.J., until Cage opens his mouth. Khaki overalls

After the usual chicken dinner, the students who have come especially to study with Merce each present a dance choreographed in class. Saturday chicken dinner Consequences: Olson very enthusiastic about the minimalist solo

A buxom, dark-haired Mediterranean student, never out of her leotards all session (the wags swore she slept in them), spends hours rubbing her back like a cat against the same pillar, pliés and ports de bras, looking ecstatic; she talks only of dance; Mary Fiore, worried, suspects an impossible dream in her, even the edge of madness; those in the know judge she has no chance as a dancer. Always the same pillar; an apologetic smile when Rumaker sweeps too close

Very tall, very thin, long spindly arms and legs, curly black hair, black-rimmed glasses, a turquoise leotard with a crêpe waist like a little girl's bathing suit: her dance, facing the audience, motionless, made of barely perceptible micro-movements of the hands and feet to modernist music of sound rather than melody, wins over Olson, who applauds loudly amid the timid applause, his face red with pleasure, praising the modesty and precision of her gestures. Consequences: Rumaker sees in it a kinship with Olson: something delicate, sharp, and small in him, the soul of Connie and later of Betty Kaiser

After the production of Zeami's Noh play staged by Wes, Olson climbs onto the stage, playfully slaps Rumaker, and mocks his priestly role: “And you—you played it like a Catholic priest!”; Rumaker, stung, wonders what other models he had, Olson included; he realizes that Olson, when he cares about you, must be the authority on everything you do.

A former student back for the 1953 Institute (with the dancer Remy Charlip, who joins Merce's class), Herlihy offers an informal class in acting exercises and technique to a handful of regular and summer students; work on scenes from Laurence Housman's Victoria Regina; very good at stage business (showing the young Victoria how to screw on...). Herlihy pronounces it “Regeena,” smiling: the other pronunciation sounds too much like “vagina”

Herlihy, a former student back for the 1953 Summer Institute with the dancer Remy Charlip, offers an informal class in acting exercises and technique in the basement of the Studies Building to a handful of students; work on scenes from Laurence Housman's Victoria Regina Herlihy pronounces “Regina” as “Regeena,” smiling: the other pronunciation sounds too much like “vagina”; he shows the young woman playing Victoria how to screw on her earrings for the best effect

Herlihy falls head over heels in love with Basil King, a Cockney painting student raised in Detroit; when Basil rebuffs him, Herlihy, crushed and humiliated, leaves the college the next day without a word to anyone Consequences: A summer stay cut short

A costume ball organized by Weinrib and M.C. Richards for Wes Huss's birthday; tableaux of the great lovers of history with Wes's drama students, a finale on the raft moored in the lake with Karen Karnes nude as Ophelia, draped in leaves and flowers Karen Karnes insists on replacing Mary Ann Fretz, whom she suspects David of wanting to see naked; Pat Nelson and Rumaker dressed as a nun and a monk (a brown bag from the 5 & 10 store, a wimple made from an old sheet from the North Lodge linen, a rosary of knotted white cord); nails painted black with India ink; Rumaker poses as Bacchus in a toga; candles on sheet-covered tables; crackling 78 rpm records on the old Magnavox by the fireplace Consequences: Wes Huss leaves the ball by the kitchen door with Pat Nelson, in her nun's habit; the next day, a rumor of a private birthday celebration in Pat's study in the Studies Building

Carried away by their sacrilegious costumes, Pat and Michael plan a Black Mass in front of the big fieldstone fireplace, with a Kyrie eleison on the little cherrywood pump organ; they give it up under the pressure of bad taste and their still-vivid Catholic fear Cherrywood foot-pumped organ, rarely played; fear of the Pope's wrath at perpetrating a sacrilege

Top down, Olson drives fast, talking over his shoulder about the California potter Peter Voulkos, who has come to learn innovation at the college while teaching at the ceramics institute that summer; he admires his big head and his dark, handsome Greek face and declares that so many geniuses have big heads Blue Ford convertible; the wind whistling in their ears; Olson conscious of his own enormous head on his broad shoulders

One Sunday afternoon, Rumaker reads his new “experiential” writing (a family's suffering during the Depression) together with the veteran Fee Dawson; a poster painted by Joe Hire pinned on the cork board; the whole community, including summer visitors; few comments afterward: no great success, but great relief Rumaker is 21; in the morning: barely any breakfast, one coffee after another, chain-smoked Home Run cigarettes, the sun rising over Lake Eden and snowcapped Mount Mitchell in the distance; Dorothea Rockburne gives him practical advice: asked what he needs to do now, he says shave, and she tells him to do it; a long walk in the hills; a pep talk from Mary on the way to the dining hall Consequences: Wolpe declares in front of him that Rumaker does not yet know how to lie; Olson hammers home this insight afterward; it bears fruit ~1 year later in the first calf story written in class; Rumaker reformulates it: the lie of the imagination creates the truth of reality

Olson declares emphatically, with a touch of sadness, that Keats was “stuck with description,” regretting what he might otherwise have done, he who had had the brilliant intuition of “negative capability,” a notion Olson was developing a great deal in class and in his writing at the time. The phrase “stuck with description”; a reference to “negative capability” Consequences: Rumaker sees in it a warning against his tendency to pile up adjectives, to describe from outside rather than be in the moment of writing.

Desperate to produce something to read in class, Rumaker writes a poem about Billie Holiday; Olson tans his hide: a “silly” poem that does justice neither to her nor to her singing. Consequences: Rumaker understands the futility of forcing his writing just to have a ticket into Olson's class.

One very cold February evening, about three years after leaving Black Mountain, Rumaker and a rich lesbian friend, with some women friends, hear Billie Holiday at the Blue Note (two sets, the money gone for a third). Walking around the block to the friend's Mercedes, they spot her through the window of an ordinary bar: flat shoes kicked off at the foot of the stool, her trademark gardenia in her hair, a glass of gin in front of her, chatting with the Black bartender. They go in; Rumaker, heart pounding, goes to order cheap draft beers. Holiday asks the bartender for a Slim Jim (heartburn all day, nothing eaten), asks him “You a college boy?”, says she wants to add “My Funny Valentine” to her repertoire without knowing the words, tests him, has him put a quarter in the jukebox for the instrumental, stands behind him, says “Sing,” then takes over and sings the song, softly, with impeccable phrasing, into his right ear. The friend's Mercedes; two sets; a quarter in the jukebox; a Slim Jim in a cellophane wrapper; gin; a gardenia in her hair; an empty bar except for her and the bartender, one leg against the sink Consequences: Rumaker remains “spellbound”: a memorable scene of a furtive encounter with his idol.

Olson says in front of the others, about Rumaker's stories, that Michael has to be serious all the time, and then that he doesn't know what he is doing when he does it anyway, aiming at his inarticulateness: no use asking him. Rumaker is troubled but knows Olson is right. Consequences: Rumaker will later recognize in “The Use of the Unconscious in Writing” that it is crucial not to be too conscious of what one is doing.

Olson advises Rumaker to follow his nose in writing, like pushing a peanut ahead of himself. He also warns him not always to be on the side of the angels, touching on his altar-boy naivete, and tacitly encourages him to dance with the devil now and then. Image: pushing a peanut ahead of oneself

One night around two or three in the morning, a gang of local toughs, probably drunk, drives onto the grounds, furiously bangs the fire gong behind the kitchen's back door shouting “Nigger lovers! Nigger lovers!”, then roars off. (Brown v. Board of Education is still a year in the future.) Around 2-3 a.m.; the gong outside the kitchen's back door Consequences: A brutal reminder of the deeply segregationist South outside the college's pagan paradise.

As everyone waits for dinner in front of the dining hall, among them a few Black guests, a big, dusty black Cadillac (an expensive car, an unusual sight at the college) pulls up with a burly white man in a soft felt hat and suspenders, an equally burly woman beside him. The driver leans over and yells through the open passenger window: “Ahm gonna report all you niggah lovahs!”, then roars around Dinner Bell Circle in a cloud of yellow dust and heads back to the county road. A big, dusty black Cadillac; a soft felt hat; suspenders; yellow dust

One hot late afternoon, several members of the college and a woman from India go to drink beer at Peak's. Once they are seated, short, plump Ma Peak comes out from behind the bar and announces in her greasy singsong: “I kin serve evahbody but you,” nodding her braided head toward the Indian visitor. Dan Rice (Rumaker believes) retorts: “But she's from India”. Ma Peak folds her arms over her ample bosom: “Look at 'er, black as a nigger.” Olson takes her aside and deploys all his persuasion; she stubbornly refuses: “Git 'er outa here! I don' want 'er in here!” Consequences: They have beers put up to go and go back to drink at the college, a reminder that the law is on Ma Peak's side. Rumaker, a homosexual, feels grateful for this haven for all the outcasts of that dreadful era.

Another evening in class, Olson declares that the tragedy of Black people is that they cannot play all out on the whole board (they are not allowed to), and that between whites and Blacks there must be a coalescence.

On a Saturday night panel devoted to contemporary music, Wolpe mentions that he is an atheist. A tall, thin blond woman in the front row, clearly from the area, shrieks her disbelief in her deep Southern accent: “You mine ta' tell me you don't believe in Gawd”. Wolpe, looking bored, his basset-hound face even more furrowed, declares flatly: “No, of course not!”, in a tone suggesting that only idiots believe in God. Scattered amused laughter, mostly from college regulars. The woman, flabbergasted, mouth agape, turns to her companions and for the rest of the discussion keeps a worried frown, as if she had entered an incredibly evil place. Wolpe's basset-hound face; Saturday night; dining hall Consequences: Rumaker, who has just been fighting with his family (especially his mother) over God and religion, is much impressed by this clean, blunt rejection.

In class in the Reading Room, Olson talks about the Church: Christianity became a dead end when it attacked sex in the 1500s, and the Church will remain out of date until the sacred has been restored to the sacrament; then he jokes about the possible death of the pope of the day. Rumaker murmurs: “There'll only be another one”. Olson, eyes shining, asks excitedly, “Who said that? Who said that?”; when Rumaker owns up, a little sheepishly, Olson smiles broadly, delighted and surprised.

In late spring 1953, one Sunday afternoon, the cook Malrey invites Rumaker and Mary Fiore to the 8th-grade graduation of her nephew Alvin. The school, entirely Black, is a building of unpainted boards at the end of a country lane, compared with the neat, more expensive white schools they pass on the way. Alvin, tall and gangly in a black suit and tie, shy, had been the Page in Satie's The Ruse of Medusa (translated by M.C. Richards) in August 1948 in the dining hall, with Buckminster Fuller and Merce Cunningham, sets by Willem and Elaine de Kooning. Mary and Rumaker, the only white people, are looked at politely and warily; they sit on stiff chairs at the back and wait until the parents have finished congratulating him before shaking Alvin's hand and thanking him for his little speech; he gives them back his shy adolescent smile. Consequences: On the way back, Rumaker thinks of all there is to learn outside the college as much as within it.

Sunday, the cooks' half day off (after lunch Malrey and Cornelia set out cheese, bread, and apples on the rolling table by the pass-through for supper). Rumaker comes down from Minimum House with Mary in her Jeep station wagon; Cornelia, in her Sunday clothes, is waiting in front of the dining hall. Rumaker invites her into the front seat between them; she stubbornly refuses, “Naw, naw, naw,” climbing into the back as quick as a sparrow. Rumaker, not understanding, jokes that he has had a bath. Mary, silent at the wheel, has understood: a Black woman in front with two white people would gravely violate the segregation code; Cornelia is doing what law and custom demand, like sitting at the back of the valley's segregated buses. They drop her off in a Black neighborhood poorer and more run-down than the poor white neighborhoods of Asheville. Mary's Jeep station wagon; cheese, bread, and apples on the rolling table; ~13 miles west toward Asheville; as quick as a sparrow Consequences: Rumaker realizes that in daily life, despite the college, they live apart: he knows almost nothing of Cornelia's and Malrey's lives, while they, sharp-eyed, know more of his.

One night shortly afterward, leaving South Lodge to write in his study, Rumaker spots a tall, thin, boyish figure crouching on the porch of North Lodge, spying on the lighted window of Virginia's bathroom: it is Alvin, in the hormonal torrents of adolescence, eager for a glimpse of female flesh. So as not to embarrass him, Rumaker slips by as quietly as Alvin and goes on toward the Studies Building, telling himself that they are two creatures hidden in the sexual shadows, his own curiosity veering resolutely toward the male side.

Bill McNeil, a painting student from New York who has recently arrived, and Rumaker size each other up and circle each other for days; Bill, gentle and quietly humorous, often comes to Rumaker's study to chat. One evening after supper they head for the Quiet House, which no one at that time still used for the prayer and meditation for which Molly Gregory and the student Alex Reed had built it in the 1940s in memory of Eddie Dreier, the Dreiers' son, killed in a car accident on campus. Once the door is shut in total darkness, his hunger is as wild as Rumaker's; they fall onto a damp bench. They meet several more times, at the Quiet House or in the study (dry, with a light and a pallet). Bill does not stay long at the college (other uncertainties in his eyes), and Rumaker, the ever-hungry animal, misses his gentle, shy humor and his pensive silence. A damp bench; a pallet in the study; Merrill then still in Houston Consequences: In the 1970s, Tom Field tells Rumaker that Bill lives in San Francisco; in the early 1980s, Don Allen (editor at Grey Fox) writes that Bill has died of AIDS, one of the first to go.

Summer 1953: Vicente teaches drawing from nude models; the students draw in pencil on large sketch sheets bought at Carroll Williams's college store. A man of few words, Vicente goes from student to student, standing straight and dignified, really studying the work, offering comments that are often abrupt, often complimentary and encouraging. Mary Ann Fretz, unusually shy, reveals a hidden exhibitionist streak by posing nude (with a shy person one can do anything but ignore her); likewise Bea Huss, just as reserved. Tim La Farge, an attractive young dancer in Merce's company, seen all summer in a black leotard in Merce's classes, is mentioned. Hairy bare chest, nothing but tight white shorts and sandals; a bull's chest; thick gray hair pulled back; craggy Mediterranean features burned reddish brown by the Carolina sun

An ancient tree is cut down, its stump removed, and a decrepit windowless wood-shingle building (lately used for painting classes) demolished. The widows Johanna Jalowetz, Nell Rice, and Toni Dehn protest vehemently; Rumaker reads in it the fear that their own precarious position at the college might be just as ruthlessly uprooted. The men (Dan Rice, Olson, Huss) mock the “old women” and go ahead anyway. Rumaker keeps the image of Jalowetz's weathered, furiously dark face when their cause is lost; debate or vote uncertain. Consequences: Resentment among the elders

Jonathan Williams, a former student, Jargon publisher, and poet, then in the army in Germany, has used a $1,500 inheritance to print in West Germany the first copies of The Maximus Poems 1-10, large volumes bound in pale blue with a big black brushstroke O. Olson shows them to the students in the grass, quietly, looking from the book to them and back, without saying anything, but his joy is plain. The poorest scrape together three dollars (saving on food and beer) to buy this beautifully printed book of a vital text by the beloved master. A $1,500 inheritance; price $3; pale blue cover, a black brushstroke O Consequences: A silent, exhilarating moment of recognition in the sun

People always came to visit Black Mountain, especially in good weather: a windfall for the single, fresh conversation, new ears, possible flirting, sometimes even sex, welcome for those short of partners, especially those of “queer” inclinations.
There is talk of abolishing the scholarships of the work program, judged undemocratic and a source of cheap labor. Consequences: Increased anxiety for Rumaker, a scholarship student.

Rumaker gives Mary Ann Fretz's address to Wes Huss at the registrar's office in the administration cottage, secretly packs his suitcase while Merrill is out, hides it under the bed, then leaves before dawn without waking anyone or saying goodbye, to hitchhike to New York. His mother's suitcase; a dollar or two in his pocket; route: the county road, Raleigh, U.S. 1 north; several hundred miles; 600 miles covered in two days; birds still silent in the predawn dark; fear of jail or the chain gang for vagrancy, Georgia the worst state, North Carolina right behind. Consequences: The end of living with Merrill after a whole first year at the college.

Arrival after two days of hitchhiking at the one-room apartment that Mary Ann (who is studying photography and mime there) offers him until he finds a job. Across the landing: a male brothel much frequented by Marines and sailors; upstairs, over a dark slate courtyard; coal soot (ConEd, East River) inches deep on the sills like black snow; chocolate brown walls; a big BMC-style pallet mattress plus a rice mat; a noisy black refrigerator, unplugged; windowsills used as a winter refrigerator; yogurt, a novelty; rent of $60 a month. Consequences: Rumaker's New York base for the winter.

Thanks to his ability to type, he becomes a mail clerk and then a telex operator at the publisher Prentice-Hall. $48 a week; walking to work through Washington Square; demolition under way on that stretch of Fifth Avenue (Mark Twain's last New York residence, the old Brevoort Café) for a vast apartment complex. Consequences: He can pay his half of the $60 rent; the apartment in effect becomes his.

Rumaker meets up again with Henry L. Wood (“Woody”), whom he met at Chautauqua in the summer of 1952, with whom he had lost his queer virginity, and pursues with him an “apprenticeship” in the pleasures of the flesh and in Culture. A rent-controlled apartment, cramped but superbly elegant, with a view of Williamsburg; trousers always well creased, tweed jackets, silk ties; Woody pays for theater and ballet, Rumaker paying later in bed; he takes him to the Astor Bar in Times Square, the city's most famous and unacknowledged gay cruising spot (the other: the Oak Room at the Plaza). Consequences: Rumaker's cultural and sexual education.
